tagline: A mountain switchback keeps the turnpike’s older line above Durbin
intro: Back Mountain Backway climbs the east side of Cheat Mountain on the original Staunton-Parkersburg Turnpike alignment. FHWA describes 2.7 miles of blacktop lined with residences and allows ten minutes for the drive. The West Virginia Encyclopedia lists it among the state-designated scenic highways. The turnpike alliance values these bypassed roads as places to interpret the original highway.
This alignment was paved in the 1920s and carried US 250 until a more direct climb replaced it in the 1950s.

From the bridge at Durbin’s west end, the old road climbs through a switchback, passes behind the ridge away from the modern highway, and rejoins it farther uphill. Small settlements remain along the turnpike line.

moments.title: The Durbin crossing
moments.text: The route appendix places the old turnpike crossing at the bridge on Durbin’s west end. At Durbin, the East and West Forks meet to form the Greenbrier River. Beyond the crossing, the original roadway begins its switchback ascent.

moments.title: The switchback
moments.text: The switchback carries Back Mountain Road onto the far side of the ridge, away from the modern highway. This is a paved remnant of the original route: the road received pavement in the 1920s and remained US 250 until the 1950s.

moments.title: Return to the highway
moments.text: Small settlements continue along the old turnpike before it rejoins the highway for the climb farther up the mountain. The change in alignment dates to the 1950s, when the more direct US 250 route replaced this road as the main highway.
